title: Putting the Gene Back to Prove Cause
endLine: If losing a gene breaks function, putting it back should restore it.

scenes.tts: When you silence a gene and the cell breaks, did losing it really cause the defect? Maybe not: a silencing tool can hit the wrong target. A rescue experiment tests cause by putting a working copy back.
scenes.caption: When you silence a gene and the cell breaks, did losing it really cause the defect? Maybe not: a silencing tool can hit the wrong target. A rescue experiment tests cause by putting a working copy back.
scenes.visual: Schematic large cell filling most of the frame height, pulsing steadily at start. A glowing gene bar dims as a silencing wedge strikes it; the cell stalls and dims with a bold question mark beside it before a bright working gene bar slides into view.
scenes.narration: When you silence a gene and the cell breaks, did losing it really cause the defect? Maybe not: a silencing tool can hit the wrong target. A rescue experiment tests cause by putting a working copy back.

scenes.tts: Normally, a gene makes messenger R N A to build a protein. A silencing guide, an s h R N A, pairs with that message. The protein vanishes, and the cell breaks. If losing it caused the defect, adding a working copy back should cure it. If an off-target hit broke it, the defect stays.
scenes.caption: Normally, a gene makes messenger RNA to build a protein. A silencing guide, an shRNA, pairs with that message. The protein vanishes, and the cell breaks. If losing it caused the defect, adding a working copy back should cure it. If an off-target hit broke it, the defect stays.
scenes.visual: Same schematic cell carried in place. First, the gene bar produces a moving mRNA ribbon and geometric protein dots (no molecular structures) while the cell pulses cleanly. An shRNA guide clamps onto the ribbon; dots fade and the cell stalls. Then two brief split outcomes from adding a copy back: dots return and cell revives (label: On-target) versus cell stays stalled (label: Off-target).
scenes.narration: Normally, a gene makes messenger RNA to build a protein. A silencing guide, an shRNA, pairs with that message. The protein vanishes, and the cell breaks. If losing it caused the defect, adding a working copy back should cure it. If an off-target hit broke it, the defect stays.

scenes.tts: There is a catch. The s h R N A is still inside the cell, ready to silence any matching message. So predict. How can a rescue copy make the exact same protein and still escape that guide?
scenes.caption: There is a catch. The shRNA is still inside the cell, ready to silence any matching message. So predict. How can a rescue copy make the exact same protein and still escape that guide?
scenes.visual: Same schematic cell. A new rescue gene bar enters and sends out an identical mRNA ribbon, but the lingering shRNA guide glides straight toward it and highlights the matching target segment. A clear high-contrast question card appears above the cell: 'How can rescue escape the shRNA?'
scenes.narration: There is a catch. The shRNA is still inside the cell, ready to silence any matching message. So predict. How can a rescue copy make the exact same protein and still escape that guide?

scenes.visual: Hold the schematic cell with the predict question on screen. Keep slow ambient motion: the shRNA guide hovers and gently pulses near the mRNA ribbon's highlighted target segment while the viewer thinks.

scenes.tts: Change the codons at the target site to synonymous codons, different codes for the same amino acid. These silent mutations alter the message, so the guide no longer pairs with it. Yet the amino-acid sequence stays the same. The protein returns, and the cell recovers.
scenes.caption: Change the codons at the target site to synonymous codons, different codes for the same amino acid. These silent mutations alter the message, so the guide no longer pairs with it. Yet the amino-acid sequence stays the same. The protein returns, and the cell recovers.
scenes.visual: Same schematic cell, zoomed gently on the rescue mRNA ribbon's target segment (schematic). Its colored block segments change pattern while keeping the same geometric protein shapes underneath (label: Synonymous codons). The shRNA guide drifts past without binding. Geometric protein dots refill the cell and its healthy pulse returns.
scenes.narration: Change the codons at the target site to synonymous codons, different codes for the same amino acid. These silent mutations alter the message, so the guide no longer pairs with it. Yet the amino-acid sequence stays the same. The protein returns, and the cell recovers.

scenes.tts: Still, a rescue can mislead if levels are wrong. A failed rescue means little unless the protein is folded, placed, and near normal levels. Far too much protein can cause effects of its own. Researchers check levels with an immunoblot, an antibody test for the protein.
scenes.caption: Still, a rescue can mislead if levels are wrong. A failed rescue means little unless the protein is folded, placed, and near normal levels. Far too much protein can cause effects of its own. Researchers check levels with an immunoblot, an antibody test for the protein.
scenes.visual: Same schematic cell shifts left while a schematic immunoblot strip appears on the right (labels: Normal, Too low, Too high). Inside the cell, protein dots dim and misplace for the failed lane, then crowd excessively for the overloaded lane, before settling at the matched normal band.
scenes.narration: Still, a rescue can mislead if levels are wrong. A failed rescue means little unless the protein is folded, placed, and near normal levels. Far too much protein can cause effects of its own. Researchers check levels with an immunoblot, an antibody test for the protein.

scenes.tts: Even a working rescue is not proof alone. Extra copies of one gene can suppress a defect in another. Overexpressed A P G one, for example, rescues an a p g thirteen mutant. Sequencing the mutant allele, or remaking the mutation in a clean strain, rules out a second hit.
scenes.caption: Even a working rescue is not proof alone. Extra copies of one gene can suppress a defect in another. Overexpressed APG1, for example, rescues an apg13 mutant. Sequencing the mutant allele, or remaking the mutation in a clean strain, rules out a second hit.
scenes.visual: Same schematic cell, now showing a broken apg13 locus (schematic). Multiple extra APG1 gene bars appear and flood geometric dots through a bypass path, restarting the cell's pulse even though apg13 stays broken. A clean check overlay highlights reading the mutant gene sequence and remaking the mutation in a fresh cell.
scenes.narration: Even a working rescue is not proof alone. Extra copies of one gene can suppress a defect in another. Overexpressed APG1, for example, rescues an apg13 mutant. Sequencing the mutant allele, or remaking the mutation in a clean strain, rules out a second hit.

scenes.tts: Used carefully, rescue reveals shared biology across species. In 1982, David Beach, Barbara Durkacz, and Paul Nurse rescued a fission-yeast c d c two mutant. They added budding-yeast D N A carrying C D C twenty-eight: two distant yeasts, one job. In 1987, a human gene rescued that same mutant.
scenes.caption: Used carefully, rescue reveals shared biology across species. In 1982, David Beach, Barbara Durkacz, and Paul Nurse rescued a fission-yeast cdc2 mutant. They added budding-yeast DNA carrying CDC28: two distant yeasts, one job. In 1987, a human gene rescued that same mutant.
scenes.visual: The schematic cell elongates smoothly into a schematic fission-yeast rod stalled before division (label: cdc2 mutant). A budding-yeast CDC28 gene bar enters (label: 1982) and the rod divides cleanly at its middle; then a human gene bar replaces it (label: 1987) and the rod divides cleanly again.
scenes.narration: Used carefully, rescue reveals shared biology across species. In 1982, David Beach, Barbara Durkacz, and Paul Nurse rescued a fission-yeast cdc2 mutant. They added budding-yeast DNA carrying CDC28: two distant yeasts, one job. In 1987, a human gene rescued that same mutant.

scenes.tts: In 2015, Aashiq Kachroo, Edward Marcotte, and colleagues tested matching human genes in place of yeast genes. Of four hundred fourteen genes yeast cannot live without, one hundred seventy-six restored growth in their assays. Dividing one hundred seventy-six by four hundred fourteen gives about forty-three percent, or forty-seven percent with earlier cases. Failed swaps do not prove lost function, since failure has several causes.
scenes.caption: In 2015, Aashiq Kachroo, Edward Marcotte, and colleagues tested matching human genes in place of yeast genes. Of 414 genes yeast cannot live without, 176 restored growth in their assays. Dividing 176 by 414 gives about 43%, or 47% with earlier cases. Failed swaps do not prove lost function, since failure has several causes.
scenes.visual: Schematic budding-yeast outline morphs smoothly into a computed horizontal bar for the 414 tested genes (label: 414 genes yeast needs). As spoken, the exact 176/414 fraction fills in with the formula '176 / 414 ≈ 43%' appearing term by term, then a second marker extends to 47%, marked "schematic" since it is not computed from these numbers (label: With earlier cases). The remaining segment stays softly shaded with a note: 'Failure has several causes'.

scenes.tts: Rescue can also show where a signal acts. In 1985, Kathryn Anderson and colleagues studied fly embryos from Toll mutant mothers. Those dorsalized embryos lack ventral, belly-side structures. Injected wild-type cytoplasm made the ventralmost part of the pattern form wherever the needle went in. Done carefully, putting the missing piece back tests true cause.

scenes.visual: The frame morphs into a large schematic fly embryo outline (label: 1985, Toll mutant mother) with uniform dorsal shading. A schematic needle injects wild-type cytoplasm at one spot and a bright ventralmost band radiates from that exact site; then a second schematic embryo is injected at a different spot and its ventralmost band forms there instead.
